name: Wilsonianism (liberal internationalism)

plain: Woodrow Wilson's idea that America should spread democracy, back national self-rule and build a league of nations so that collective security replaces the balance of power.
summary: Wilson's World War I program: democracy promotion, self-determination, open diplomacy and collective security through a League of Nations; revived in later US policy.

rationale.christianity: Wilson's Presbyterian upbringing shaped 'a worldview integrating religious ethics with governance' (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Universal democracy, consent and collective security; echoes 'Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty' (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.marxism: A liberal rival to revolutionary socialism after 1917; not defined by anticommunism the way later Cold War strands were.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.nationalism: National self-determination is a core plank: Points 9–14 sought polities for nationalities under imperial rule (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Builds world order 'on moral and legalistic foundations rather than balance-of-power realism' (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).
rationale.hierarchy: Favors law, open covenants and collective security among nations over great-power spheres (Grokipedia, Wilsonianism).

places.note: Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 1918) and war message (1917) set the doctrine as US policy.
Wilson pressed the program at the Paris Peace Conference, the program 'inspiring the League of Nations covenant'.
The UN Charter (1945) directly inheriting the League of Nations' structure for collective security; the UN sits in New York.

enlightenment_liberalism.note: Self-determination 'derived from consent-based governance, echoing Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty but applied internationally'.

calvinism.note: Wilson grew up in 'a strict Calvinist environment' as a Presbyterian minister's son; the page ties this to his moral view of governance.

parent_note: Liberal internationalism is merged here as an alias: Grokipedia says it 'crystallized as a coherent doctrine during World War I under U.S. President Woodrow Wilson'. Its 19th-century free-trade forerunners are not split out.

name: Cold War liberal anticommunism
origin_note: Americans for Democratic Action was 'founded in 1947' by Eleanor Roosevelt, Hubert Humphrey, Arthur Schlesinger Jr., Reinhold Niebuhr and others 'to advance non-communist progressive policies'; Truman announced his doctrine on March 12, 1947; Schlesinger's The Vital Center followed in 1949
plain: Postwar Democrats who kept the New Deal at home and fought communism abroad: Truman's containment, the ADA and Schlesinger's 'vital center' between left and right extremes.
summary: Postwar liberalism that paired New Deal welfare with anticommunist containment; Truman, ADA (1947), Schlesinger's Vital Center (1949), later Scoop Jackson.

rationale.christianity: Reinhold Niebuhr, a Protestant theologian, co-founded ADA (Grokipedia, ADA); the movement itself was secular in program.
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Vital-center liberalism stressed 'individual integrity, pluralism' and democratic freedom (Grokipedia, Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.).
rationale.marxism: Founded 'to advance non-communist progressive policies' (Grokipedia, ADA); containment of Soviet communism is its core.
rationale.critical_theory: No real link to critical theory.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: No real link to Islamic philosophy (falsafa).
rationale.nationalism: Patriotic defense of the free world; Jackson stressed 'military strength' against Soviet expansion (Grokipedia, Henry M. Jackson).
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Makes its case directly, without ironic distance.
rationale.abstraction: Schlesinger grounded it in 'empirical recognition of human imperfection' (Grokipedia, Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr.).
rationale.hierarchy: Backed a strong national-security state abroad while extending welfare and labor protections at home (Grokipedia, Henry M. Jackson).

places.note: Truman's March 12, 1947 address committed aid to Greece and Turkey against communist pressure.
Jackson's Coalition for a Democratic Majority (May 1972) sought 'to reclaim the party from New Left influences'.

new_deal_liberalism.note: ADA's founders, New Deal Democrats, organized after FDR's death to keep liberalism non-communist; The Vital Center defended the New Deal against totalitarianism.

wilsonianism.note: The Truman Doctrine framed containment 'as an extension of Wilsonian self-determination and democratic expansion against Soviet influence'.

parent_note: Grokipedia has no 'Cold War liberalism' or 'Vital Center' article; the node rests on ADA, Schlesinger, Truman Doctrine, Jackson and Neoconservatism pages. Reinhold Niebuhr is an ADA founder but has no node.

name: Straussian political philosophy
origin_note: Dated to 1949, when Strauss took up a professorship at Chicago, where he 'cultivated a dedicated following of students through seminars focused on primary texts'; Natural Right and History (1953) set out his defense of 'timeless natural right'; 'By the time of Strauss's death in 1973, his students had formed a self-sustaining intellectual movement'
plain: Leo Strauss and his students: careful reading of Plato and the classics, a belief in natural right against modern relativism, and the claim that philosophers often wrote between the lines.
summary: Leo Strauss's recovery of classical political philosophy: natural right against historicism, esoteric reading of Plato, Farabi and Maimonides, and a school of students.

rationale.platonism: Defends 'timeless natural right grounded in reason and classical sources like Plato' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.aristotelianism: Draws 'from Plato, Aristotle, and Machiavelli' for classical political philosophy (Grokipedia, Neoconservatism).
rationale.christianity: Frames the issue as philosophy versus revelation, Athens versus Jerusalem, without taking a Christian side (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.enlightenment_liberalism: Defends liberal democracy against totalitarianism but critiques modernity's break 'from classical natural right' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.marxism: Treats modern historicism, Marxism's frame included, as leading to relativism and nihilism (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.nietzsche: Casts Nietzsche and Heidegger as the 'third wave' of modernity that ends in nihilism (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.critical_theory: Opposes historicist reduction of moral standards to 'cultural artifacts' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss); no direct engagement.
rationale.islamic_philosophy: Read Al-Farabi as an esoteric writer and began with research on 'medieval Islamic philosophy' (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.judaism: Born to 'an observant Jewish family'; read Maimonides' Guide and wrote on philosophy versus revelation and Zionism (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.nationalism: No real link to nationalism.
rationale.humor: Not expressed through jokes or play.
rationale.irony: Holds that philosophers wrote esoterically, hiding meanings beneath an exoteric surface (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).
rationale.abstraction: Holds that enduring truths about human nature and the best regime 'can be discerned through reason' (Grokipedia, Neoconservatism).
rationale.hierarchy: Critics such as Drury see 'a stark natural hierarchy' of philosophers over the many; the page also records rebuttals (Grokipedia, Leo Strauss).

places.note: Strauss taught there from 1949 and built a following of students around close reading of primary texts.
His students formed 'a self-sustaining intellectual movement' by 1973 that revived great-books education.

platonic_forms.note: Strauss defended 'timeless natural right grounded in reason and classical sources like Plato' and taught seminars on Plato's texts.

aristotelian_teleology.note: Strauss 'emphasized the enduring truths of classical political philosophy—drawing from Plato, Aristotle, and Machiavelli'.

falsafa.note: He began in 1932 researching 'medieval Islamic philosophy in Paris' and read Al-Farabi as veiling 'critiques of prophetic authority under apparent deference'.

parent_note: Strauss read Nietzsche and Heidegger as the 'third wave' of modernity culminating in nihilism, and his engagement with Heidegger was 'adversarial'; foils, not parents, so no edges. Maimonides has no node.
